is_houseplant — removed on audit: All three supporting citations describe OUTDOOR/garden container use, not indoor houseplant suitability. MOBOT's quote is a 'Garden Uses' tag list ('Borders, path edging, cottage gardens or herb gardens... Containers...') where 'Containers' sits alongside explicitly outdoor landscape categories — it means patio/garden containers, not indoor pots. NC State's quote ('consider growing it in a container') is offered as a fix for the plant becoming 'weedy' in the garden, not as evidence of indoor cultivation. Clemson's quote ('cage them with chicken wire or grow in hanging baskets') is explicitly a way to keep outdoor plants safe from cats scratching them out of the ground, not a houseplant recommendation. Nepeta cataria is a hardy perennial (the same sources give USDA zones 3-9 and full-sun/part-shade garden culture) conventionally grown outdoors. None of the cited text states or implies the species is grown indoors as a houseplant; 'container-tolerant' has been conflated with 'houseplant.'

soil_base — removed on audit: The citation bundles 'soil_base garden_bed' onto the RHS quote 'Grow in any well-drained soil in full sun,' which supports full_sun and fast drainage but says nothing about planting location — no mention of garden bed, ground planting, or container versus bed. The value is asserted without textual support in the cited quote (re-verified by direct fetch of the RHS page, which returned sun/soil-type/pH/name-status content but no statement about bed vs. container placement).

name_note — removed on audit: The note claims sources use 'catmint' as an alternate name while 'reserving catnip as the name most specific to N. cataria' versus ornamental hybrids like N. x faassenii. A direct fetch of the NC State page shows it lists three common names for this exact species page with no hierarchy or distinction: 'Catmint, Catnip, Catswort.' The specific claim that these sources draw a catnip-vs-catmint specificity distinction is not established by the actual page text — it reads as the compiler's own botanical gloss presented as if sourced from RHS/NC State.

records.cool_rest_note: RHS: when kept indoors over winter, low light slows growth, so water sparingly; bring indoors before overnight temps fall below 45°F (7°C) and keep it above that threshold.
records.name_note: RHS lists Cymbopogon citratus with "Name Status: Correct," confirming it is the currently accepted binomial (not a synonym needing correction); RHS records Andropogon citratus as a synonym of it.

unknowns: light_fc_min / light_fc_good: only qualitative sun-exposure categories (full sun / part shade) are given by these outdoor-garden sources; no footcandle values stated.
soil_ph_min / soil_ph_max: RHS states pH tolerance qualitatively as 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' (i.e. broadly tolerant) but gives no numeric pH range.

soil_base: sources describe growing it both in containers (peat-free loam-based/multi-purpose compost) and directly in garden beds (fertile, free-draining soil); left null rather than force a single category when both settings are equally well supported.

fertilize_interval_days / fertilize_active_months: RHS gives a qualitative schedule ('every two or three weeks from spring until late summer') but not a single day-interval number or specific month set, so left null rather than collapse a stated range into false precision.

day_f_min / day_f_max: RHS states lemongrass 'needs temperatures of at least 13°C (55°F)' to thrive, but this is a general growing threshold, not clearly distinguished as a daytime-specific figure, so left null.
water_growing_days_est / water_dormant_days_est / water_check_depth_cm: no source gives a watering-frequency day count or soil-probe depth for this species.
humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max: RHS states 'moderate humidity' qualitatively but gives no percentage figures.
toxicity mechanism/plant part: NC State tags the species as a pet/horse problem but does not specify which compound or plant part is responsible, or what symptoms result.

chill_damage_f — removed on audit: The only citation (RHS 'grow-your-own' page, Winter protection section) never states that damage/injury occurs at 45°F. It is a gardener's protective action-threshold: 'bring it indoors in autumn, before overnight temperatures fall below 7°C (45°F)... place it in a bright position where temperatures remain above 7°C (45°F)' — a conservative safety margin for when to move a container plant, not a stated chilling-injury point. The word 'damage'/'injury' never appears on the page. The same RHS page elsewhere gives a different, higher active-growth threshold ('lemon grass needs temperatures of at least 13°C (55°F)' to thrive), showing the source itself does not treat 45°F as the injury boundary. The value 45 is simply the same number lifted from the night_f_min citation and reused for a physiologically distinct field the source never addresses. Additionally, the cited page (rhs.org.uk/herbs/lemongrass/grow-your-own) is explicitly a shared guide covering two different species under the common name 'Lemongrass' ('The most widely available lemon grass is Cymbopogon citratus, although you may sometimes find the slightly more compact East Indian lemon grass, C. flexuosus'), so the number is not clearly validated as specific to C. citratus.

night_f_min — removed on audit: Same underlying quote as chill_damage_f: 'bring it indoors...before overnight temperatures fall below 7°C (45°F)... place it where temperatures remain above 7°C (45°F).' This is a recommended protective threshold for gardeners, not a measured minimum survivable temperature — the actual point at which the plant would be harmed is left unstated by the source and could be lower or higher than 45°F. The source page is also a general 'Lemongrass' guide that explicitly covers two Cymbopogon species (C. citratus and C. flexuosus) under one set of instructions without differentiating temperature tolerance between them, so the figure is not clearly established as specific to C. citratus.

humidity_need — removed on audit: The cited RHS 'Cultivation' sentence — 'Grow under glass in peat-free, loam-based compost in full light with moderate humidity' — is not unique species-specific research. The identical sentence (verified via web search and confirmed content) appears verbatim on RHS's separate profile page for the congener Cymbopogon flexuosus (rhs.org.uk/plants/45988/cymbopogon-flexuosus/details): 'Cymbopogon flexuosus should be grown under glass in peat-free, loam-based compost in full light with moderate humidity.' This is stock glasshouse-cultivation boilerplate RHS applies across the genus (at minimum), not an empirically-derived, species-specific humidity requirement for C. citratus. Mapping this generic sentence to humidity_need='average' presents genus-level cultivation boilerplate as a species-specific fact.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: The RHS citation used to support soil_drainage (the one whose quote begins 'Prepare your growing site by removing any weeds and digging in two bucketfuls of organic matter...to improve moisture retention') is labeled 'free-draining soil amended with organic matter specifically for moisture retention' — but the word 'free-draining' (or any drainage claim) never appears in that quote. I fetched the live RHS page (rhs.org.uk/vegetables/globe-artichokes/grow-your-own) and confirmed the quoted sentence is only about organic matter and moisture retention; the phrase 'warmth, full sun and free-draining soil' is a separate sentence elsewhere on the page, which the record already (correctly) quotes verbatim in a DIFFERENT citation for outdoor_sun_exposure. So this citation's label asserts a fact ('free-draining') that its own quote does not state — exactly the label/quote mismatch the audit is meant to catch, even though the soil_drainage value itself happens to be independently supported by the NC State and Missouri Botanical Garden citations, both of which do say 'well-drained' in their own quoted text.

scientific_name_accepted — removed on audit: The name_note asserts, as settled fact, that 'Cynara scolymus is now treated as a synonym folded into Cynara cardunculus (Scolymus Group).' I fetched RHS's own live plant-database page at the exact URL this same record cites elsewhere (citations for hardiness/H5 and soil pH): https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/5192/cynara-scolymus/details. Its <h1> heading and <title> are 'Cynara scolymus' — RHS is currently using Cynara scolymus as the primary/accepted name for this entry, not listing it as a folded-in synonym of Cynara cardunculus (Scolymus Group); 'Cynara cardunculus' does not appear anywhere on that page's body text. So one of the record's own admissible sources, used elsewhere in the same record, does not reflect the synonymy the name_note presents as settled. The NC State and MOBOT quotes backing name_note are accurate on their own terms, but the confident 'is now treated as' framing overstates how uniformly current usage has actually shifted, given the record's own RHS citations.

night_f_min/night_f_max: not addressed by any consulted source.

chill_damage_f: RHS notes 'late frosts can damage young shoots in spring' and its plant-details page says to 'avoid frost pockets as spears are tender,' confirming frost sensitivity qualitatively, but no source gives a specific damage-threshold temperature.

toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail: NC State's toxicity entry is explicitly headed 'Poisonous to Humans' (contact dermatitis from raw shoots, GI upset from berries); RHS's 'Potentially harmful' note ('Fruits are harmful if eaten') does not name pets or animals either. No consulted source addresses toxicity to pets specifically, so this was left null rather than inferred from the human food-safety information.
humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: not addressed by any consulted source for this outdoor garden crop.
light_fc_min/light_fc_good: sources describe light only as sun-hour/full-sun-vs-shade categories (captured in outdoor_sun_exposure and direct_sun_hours_max), never as footcandle values.

fertilize_active_months/fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_strength: Clemson, UMD, RHS, and UGA all describe fertilizer timing only qualitatively ('early spring before spears emerge', 'side-dress after harvest'), without a specific calendar month, day interval, or dose-strength term.

water_check_depth_cm/water_dry_down_target: sources describe irrigation depth for watering (e.g., UGA: moisten soil to 6-8 inches) rather than a moisture-check-before-watering protocol, so these fields don't apply as defined here.
water_dormant_days_est: no source gives a watering frequency for the plant's dormant winter period (crowns are dormant underground after the ferns die back at frost).

soil_drainage — removed on audit: Value is "moderate", but no admissible source uses that word or anything like it, and the sources actually describe two SEPARATE properties that the researcher averaged together. The PSU quote cited says "soils that are not compacted, have good drainage, and hold moisture well" -- "good drainage" is the drainage-rate statement, "hold moisture well" is a separate moisture-retention statement (already captured by water_regime=keep_moist). I fetched NC State's live asparagus page directly and its own structured Cultural Conditions field reads "Soil Drainage: Good Drainage, Moist" -- these are two distinct checkbox entries from NC State's controlled vocabulary, not a single "moderate" rating. Folding a moisture-retention fact into the drainage field to land on a middle enum value is a category error that double-counts the moisture information and downgrades the drainage rate below what every source states (good/well-drained, not moderate). This is not a one-off judgment call: this exact codebase's own prior audits removed the identical "moderate (well-drained but moisture-holding)" pattern from at least two other species in app/data/verified/b6-core-gaps.json (lines ~563, ~1021) and app/data/verified/b5-edible-and-garden.json (line 85, in the very same batch category as this asparagus record), each time citing the same NC State "Good Drainage / Moist" two-tag structure as the tell. Failure direction: a soil recommended as merely 'moderate' drainage steers a grower toward a heavier, slower-draining bed mix than an extension-recommended free-draining bed for a crown crop that is notably prone to crown/root rot in wet soil.

direct_sun_hours_max — removed on audit: Value is 10, sourced from UGA's and UMD's outdoor SITE-SELECTION guidance ("eight to 10 hours of sunlight"), but this field is not used that way anywhere else in the catalog. The model's own code comment (app/models/models.py:288-293) frames direct_sun_hours_max as one of two INDOOR light axes alongside light_fc_min/light_fc_good -- "ambient intensity in footcandles, and direct-beam tolerance" -- used to predict window-scorch risk for houseplants ("Pothos and Peace Lily share an intensity need and differ on beam hours"). Every other record in the verified catalog that populates this field is a houseplant (is_houseplant=true) and the value is always 0 (checked across b1, b2, b3, b4, b6 -- 10 records, all direct_sun_hours_max=0, none positive). Every garden-bed record across the fully audited b5-edible-and-garden.json and b7-culinary-herbs.json batches (16 records: Tomato, Kale, Mint, Melon, Sunflower, Pumpkin, Peony, Myrtle, Basil, Chives, Dill, Parsley, Sage, Cilantro, Oregano, Thyme) leaves this field null, and the audited rationale for Tomato explicitly says converting an outdoor full-sun rating into this field "would be a category error." The asparagus record is the only one in the catalog that repurposes this field to mean 'hours of desirable outdoor sun' rather than 'indoor direct-beam scorch tolerance' -- the fact that outdoor_sun_exposure already correctly carries full_sun/part_shade for this species shows the intended field for that information was used correctly elsewhere, while direct_sun_hours_max was filled with a number that means something different everywhere else it appears.

water_growing_days_est — removed on audit: Value is 7 (labeled an estimate, built from UGA's "approximately 1 inch of water every week"), but this directly contradicts an established, audited convention in this same codebase for exactly this class of plant. Every single garden_bed record in the fully-verified b5-edible-and-garden.json batch (Tomato, Kale, Mint, Melon, Sunflower, Pumpkin, Peony, Myrtle) and every garden_bed record in b7-culinary-herbs.json leaves water_growing_days_est null, with the audited rationale stated explicitly in the Tomato record's unknowns: "in-ground garden crop, so interval is driven by weather and soil, not a pot/medium assumption we can state. water_regime carries the real fact." The asparagus record breaks that unanimous pattern. The underlying UGA sentence is itself a rainfall-supplement instruction ("in the absence of rain, providing approximately 1 inch of water every week" via trickle irrigation) -- not a fixed calendar interval -- so converting it into a standing 7-day reminder for an outdoor bed asserts a schedule no source states and the catalog's own convention says cannot be honestly stated for a garden crop. water_estimate_basis inherits the same problem since it exists only to justify this number. Failure direction: a user who waters on a rigid 7-day timer regardless of actual rainfall over-waters during wet stretches (risking the crown/root rot asparagus is prone to in slow-draining or waterlogged soil) and under-waters during dry ones.

records.name_note: Phaseolus vulgaris is itself the currently accepted binomial for the common bean/green bean/snap bean; no synonym substitution was needed. NC State's Plant Toolbox lists this same species under the common names Bean, Beans, Bush Bean, Green Bean, Green Beans, Pole Bean, Snap Bean, and String Bean.
records.toxicity_detail: Raw or undercooked pods/beans are toxic. The RHS listing for this species carries a "Pets (dogs)" warning that raw pods/beans are harmful if eaten. NC State's toxicity note (for humans, on the same species) attributes raw-bean toxicity to phytohaemagglutinin, a lectin concentrated in raw/undercooked seeds (especially kidney beans); cooking destroys the toxin. No source specified an exception for cooked beans as fed to pets, so this record follows the sources' literal "raw pods/beans" framing.
unknowns: chill_damage_f: Clemson ("the plants are killed by light frost") and RHS's H2 hardiness rating ("not surviving being frozen") describe frost sensitivity qualitatively but neither states a specific damage-onset temperature in °F, so this was left null rather than inferring 32°F.

soil_base: sources describe general soil fertility/drainage (fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained) but NC State notes bush beans also do fine in containers, so no single ground-bed/raised-bed/container category was assumed.
humidity_need / humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max: no source on the approved domain list discusses ambient humidity for this outdoor crop.

light_fc_min / light_fc_good: extension sources describe sun only as a duration/category (full sun, 6-10 hours/day), never as a footcandle intensity, consistent with this being an outdoor garden crop.

fertilize_interval_days / fertilize_active_months / fertilize_strength: Clemson gives fertilizer timed to plant stage (5-10-10 before planting, then a 34-0-0 sidedress before first bloom) rather than a recurring day interval, calendar months, or strength fraction, so none of these fields map cleanly to that guidance.
night_f_min / night_f_max: no source gave a nighttime-specific temperature range; only a general growing-temperature range (60-75°F) was found.

water_check_depth_cm / water_growing_days_est / water_dormant_days_est / water_estimate_basis: Clemson gives a watering depth target (moisten soil to 6 inches deep) rather than a moisture-check depth, and no source gives a day-count watering interval for garden-grown beans.
soil_ph is given as a numeric range only by Clemson (5.8-6.5); RHS separately categorizes the species as preferring "Alkaline or Neutral" soil, a qualitative label not merged into the numeric field.

direct_sun_hours_max — removed on audit: The UMD page 'Growing Beans in a Home Garden' is confirmed (via fetch) to be a multi-species guide covering snap beans (P. vulgaris), lima beans, pole beans, scarlet runner beans (P. coccineus), fava beans (Vicia faba — a different genus), southern peas and asparagus beans (Vigna spp.) under one shared set of instructions. The 'prefers 8-10 hours/day' sun line is not attributed to any single species in the source — it is crop-category guidance. Taking the upper bound of that shared figure (10) as a Phaseolus-vulgaris-specific value is the genus/class-level-figure-presented-as-species-value failure the audit brief calls out, since fava beans and southern peas are not even congeneric with green beans.

water_regime — removed on audit: Same sourcing problem as direct_sun_hours_max: the 'Keep the root zone moist by watering deeply and regularly during dry periods' line sits in the same undifferentiated multi-species UMD 'Beans' guide (snap, lima, fava, runner, southern pea, asparagus bean) with no per-species breakout, confirmed by fetching the page. It cannot be confirmed as evidence about Phaseolus vulgaris specifically rather than the general bean-crop category. Since water_regime is one of the highest-stakes fields (wrong values can kill a plant through over/under-watering), sourcing it to crop-category rather than species-specific guidance should be treated as unsound.

chill_damage_f: no source gives a specific frost/cold-damage threshold in °F for the beet root or foliage; RHS's H7 rating is an overall winter-hardiness zone rating for the species as a whole, not an actionable damage temperature for the crop.
cool_rest_note: not discussed by any source; beets are grown as an annual/biennial crop and no source describes a cool-rest/dormancy husbandry practice.

water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_check_depth_cm, water_dry_down_target, water_estimate_basis: sources state beets need 'consistent moisture' but none give a watering-interval, soil-check-depth, or dry-down schedule to estimate from.
fertilize_active_months, fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_strength: no admissible source gives a fertilizing schedule or dilution strength for beets.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: Record sets soil_drainage='moderate', citing NC State's narrative text 'moist, rich, well-drained soil.' But NC State's own structured attribute field on that exact page literally reads 'Soil Drainage: Good Drainage Moist' — not 'moderate.' Verified directly against the live page: the Cultural Conditions block lists 'Soil Drainage: Good Drainage Moist' alongside 'Soil Texture: High Organic Matter.' 'Well-drained'/'Good Drainage' would normally map to a 'good' drainage category, not 'moderate' — the researcher supplied a value the source doesn't support and that contradicts the source's own explicit categorical field.

is_houseplant — removed on audit: The MOBOT quote cited ('Best grown in moist, fertile, organically rich, light to sandy, well-drained soils in full sun. Tolerates light shade.') is purely a statement of outdoor cultivation preferences — it never says anything about whether the plant can or can't be grown as a houseplant. Nothing in the quote states or implies 'not a houseplant'; the researcher inferred the value from an unrelated statement rather than citing a source that actually addresses indoor/houseplant suitability. Fails criterion 1 (quote doesn't literally state the claimed value) even though the underlying conclusion (a root vegetable isn't grown as a houseplant) happens to be common-sense true.

name_note — removed on audit: The name_note asserts '(RHS classifies it more precisely as Beta vulgaris subsp. vulgaris, "root beet")' but no citation in the citations list supports this. The only citation attached to name_note is the Missouri Botanical Garden quote, which describes the 'Garden Beet or Beetroot Group' and never mentions RHS, the subsp. vulgaris designation, or the term 'root beet' anywhere. I checked RHS's own beetroot growing-guide page directly (rhs.org.uk/vegetables/beetroot) — it gives only the binomial 'Beta vulgaris,' no subspecies designation and no use of the phrase 'root beet.' This is an uncited factual/taxonomic assertion smuggled into a field that otherwise carries a legitimate citation, on a claim admissible only if separately sourced from rhs.org.uk, which was never done.

water_regime — removed on audit: The primary NC State citation for water_regime ('need consistent moisture in order to produce a good crop,' specific to the Garden Beet Group page) is sound and independently supports 'keep_moist.' But the second, 'supporting' MOBOT citation ('For proper growth, species plants generally need regular and consistent moisture...') is explicitly genus/species-wide boilerplate — verified verbatim on the MOBOT page, which covers Beta vulgaris as a whole (chard, sugar beet, fodder beet, and garden beet together) and which itself immediately instructs readers: 'For specific growing instructions on growing plants within each Cultivar Group of this species, consult the specific recommendations applicable to the Group of the plant being grown.' Using this species-wide, self-disclaimed passage as corroborating evidence for a Garden-Beet-Group-specific value is exactly the genus-level-generality-presented-as-species-value pattern the audit calls out, even though it doesn't end up changing the final value since the primary citation already covers it.

records.name_note: Given name "Brassica oleracea var. italica" is the standard botanical variety name for broccoli and is retained as the accepted name here. One admissible source (NC State Extension Plant Toolbox) instead files broccoli under "Brassica oleracea Cauliflower & Broccoli Group" and lists "Italica Group" as a common-name synonym for this crop, reflecting the alternate cultivar-Group naming convention some references use for Brassica crops. This is a naming-convention difference, not a taxonomic synonym replacement, so scientific_name_accepted was left matching scientific_name_given.
unknowns: chill_damage_f: no admissible source states a frost/cold-damage onset temperature for broccoli; sources (Clemson, UMD) discuss bolting (seed-stalk formation) triggered by cold, which is a different phenomenon from injury/damage, so this was not used.

toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail: NC State Plant Toolbox tags the plant group '#problem for horses' with zero elaboration (no mechanism, plant part, or confirmation for cats/dogs specifically), which is too thin to support a pet-toxicity claim in either direction.
humidity_need / humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max: none of the fetched extension pages state an ambient humidity requirement for broccoli (typical for an outdoor garden vegetable).

light_fc_min / light_fc_good / direct_sun_hours_max: sources describe sun requirement only as a duration category (full sun, 6+ hours/day) rather than a footcandle or precise-hours target beyond the category definition itself, so no numeric value was recorded; outdoor_sun_exposure captures this instead.
night_f_min / night_f_max: sources give only a combined 'average temperature' range (65-75F, Clemson) without a day/night split.

water_check_depth_cm / water_dry_down_target: no source frames watering as a moisture-check-then-water rule (common for houseplants); Clemson describes moistening the soil to a depth of 6 inches, which is a watering-depth target, not a pre-watering check depth, so it wasn't mapped to this field.
water_dormant_days_est / cool_rest_note: broccoli is grown as an annual crop harvested to maturity, and no source frames it as having a dormant/rest period, so these were left null.

fertilize_active_months / fertilize_strength: sources give fertilizer amounts and a monthly cadence but no specific calendar months (planting windows vary widely by region/season) or a dilution-strength framing.

scientific_name_accepted: only NC State's alternate 'Italica Group' naming convention was found among admissible sources; no source flagged var. italica as an outdated/replaced synonym, so the accepted name was left unchanged (see name_note).

soil_drainage — removed on audit: The sole support for 'moisture_retentive' is the NC State Plant Toolbox page for 'Brassica oleracea Cauliflower & Broccoli Group', which documents cauliflower and broccoli jointly on one shared group page rather than broccoli exclusively (the record's own name_note acknowledges this page uses a cultivar-Group naming convention covering more than just broccoli). No independent broccoli-specific source corroborates the 'Moist' drainage tag, so this is class/group-level data being presented as a broccoli-specific soil_drainage value -- the exact failure pattern the audit flags as most common.

outdoor_sun_exposure — removed on audit: The RHS quote says broccoli grows 'in sun or very light shade.' 'Very light shade' is a substantially lighter category than the standard 'part_shade' garden-exposure tag (which typically implies several hours of shade or filtered light through the day), so mapping this wording onto 'part_shade' overstates the shade tolerance the source actually states. The full_sun component of this field is independently well-supported by NC State and UMD broccoli-specific text, but the part_shade component rests on a mismatched category translation from a single UK source.

fertilize_interval_days — removed on audit: The UGA quote states fertilizer is applied 'each month during the growing season' -- the numeral 30 never appears in the quote. Per the audit's own re-derivation rule, a number in the claim label that is not literally present in the quote (and is not a plainly-stated unit conversion of the same quantity, like inches to cm) is a refutable defect regardless of whether the underlying approximation is reasonable. 'Month' was silently converted to '30 days' without that conversion being stated in the source.
records.water_estimate_basis: Estimate assumes an in-ground garden bed (not a container), established plants during the active growing season. UGA Extension states to irrigate every four to five days as needed to keep plants healthy; this field uses 5 (the upper end of that stated range) as an approximate estimate, not a measured figure.
